newsitem.title: USA: US ATTACHE REPORT - NICARAGUAN BEEF OUTPUT RISES.
newsitem.headline: US ATTACHE REPORT - NICARAGUAN BEEF OUTPUT RISES.

text.p: Here is an annual report on Nicaraguan livestock prepared by an agricultural attache with the U.S. Embassy in Nicaragua and released by the the U.S. Agriculture Department on Monday.
Attache reports are not considered official USDA data.
ANNUAL LIVESTOCK REPORT: NICARAGUA
During Calendar Year 1996, total Nicaraguan beef output reached about 49,100 MT, representing a 2.8-percent increase over the previous year's beef production.

Despite problems faced by the Nicaraguan Livestock Industry, cattle ranching can be a profitable business and its performance is used as a key economic indicator of the country. 327,500 head were slaughtered in 1996, a 1.7 percent increase compared to the previous year. According to the industry, of the total 1996 slaughter, about 42 percent were heifers, compared to 39 percent the previous year.
Nicaragua exported $41.5 million worth of beef in 1996 compared to $55.7 million in 1995, or a 25-percent drop in beef exports, caused primarily by low international beef prices.

The local industry is seeking out new markets with more attractive prices, and, in this regard, has been in touch with the Government of Mexico to include Nicaraguan beef supply in negotiations for a future trade agreement expected in 1998. In addition to beef exports to the United States under the U.S. tariff-rate quota, Nicaragua continued to export regular beef and offal to the n eighboring countries of El Salvador, Guatemala and Costa Rica.

The outlook for the next 3 to 5 years for beef exports is similar to 1995 and 1996. The sector industry is likely to continue exporting live animals (some unofficially) to Costa Rica and Honduras. Commodity Outlook, PRODUCTION
Nicaraguan cattle production (calf Crop) was 388,000 head in 1996. This is expected to climb slightly this year and next.

Municipal slaughter is primarily for domestic consumption.
From January through April 1997, industrial slaughterhouses processed 63,500 head, compared to 58,500 head the previous year in the same comparative period.
From January through April 1997, Municipal slaughterhouses processed 56,800 head compared to 52,000 during the same period in 1996.
In 1996, the average slaughter weight was 392 kg/head (864 lbs) for industrial plants, and 364.6 kg/head (804 lbs) for municipal slaughterhouses, respectively.
FEED AND PASTURE CONDITIONS
Although there is some use of feed concentrate, the majority of local cattlemen prefer to grass feed to reduce costs of production.

During 1996, local cattlemen enjoyed good rainfall patterns, allowing the cattle herd to reach acceptable slaughter weights for the traditionally heavy slaughter period from September through March. Although a few cattlemen use irrigation systems during the dry season (December through April), most use little in the way of advanced agronomic practices to maintain pasture.
The Department of Forage and Grass Seed in the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MAG) is trying to improve existing grass varieties, but little progress has been achieved up to now.

In 1992, USDA/APHIS began to implement the Screwworm Eradication Program, which is 15 percent funded by the Nicaraguan Government, and 85 percent funded by the U.S. Government. The program was originally scheduled to end in June 1996, and re-scheduled again to end in December of the same year. It now looks like it might end in June 1998, but current sterile fly production problems in Mexico may affect this time table. The program employs about 300 people in 10 locations. It is estimated that completion of this program will bring about US$11 million of benefits annually through improved added value (better hides and skins, better quality beef) and through lower costs of production (veterinary, labor). The cost of the program to date has been about US$70.5 million.
TRADE

In 1996, Nicaragua exported 3,310,760 kgs of live animals or about 8,489 bovines worth $2.7 million, mainly to El Salvador, Honduras, Guatemala, Costa Rica and Mexico. A similar quantity was exported to the same countries in the previous year.

In 1996, total Nicaraguan beef exports totaled about $41.5 million and 22,460 MT, compared to $55.7 million and 26,197 MT beef exports from the previous year. Exports to the United States accounted for 8,400 MT in 1996.

Declining international beef prices in 1996 limited Nicaragua's ability to export more beef to the United States. This was partially responsible for encouraging local cattlemen to search for of better prices by to smuggling live animals to Costa Rica and Honduras.

The outlook for 1997 beef exports is for export levels similar to 1996, due to low international prices and, consequently, attractive live animal prices. EXPORT OPPORTUNITIES FOR ANIMAL GENETICS

Good opportunities exist for poultry and livestock genetics. In 1996, U.S. exports of hatching eggs to Nicaragua reached $2.8 million. The U.S. also exported baby breeding chicks for broilers valued at $105,000. The country imported $65,000 worth of livestock genetics and $185,000 worth of live animals, during the same period (CY96). Future Livestock imports from the United States, will depend on price and credit terms, especially for live animals. Since 1993, Nicaraguan cattlemen have benefitted from training supported under USDA's Emerging Markets Program.
EXPORT OPPORTUNITIES FOR TALLOW

In 1996, U.S. exports of animal fats to Nicaragua totaled $6.9 million and 13,143 MT. From 1993 through 1995, the U.S. enjoyed almost 100 -percent market share for Nicaragua's tallow imports. Much of this came under PL-480, Title III Program donations. No donations are expected in 1997, with Nicaragua expected to fill its demand through commercial purchases. Nicaragua produces only about 3,000 MT of tallow a year, and normally consumes about 20,000 MT.
